understanding the role of different belowground processes in the carbon cycle and their relationship with the aboveground processes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
soil respiration is not a simple linear function of temperature and photosynthesis.
the relationship between respiration sources and photosynthesis is not straightforward and requires a more detailed analysis at the ecosystem level.
the partitioning of soil CO2 efflux is a useful tool to understand belowground carbon cycling, especially when combined with eddy covariance data to study the relationship with aboveground processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
soil respiration fluxes are highly dependent on the forest type, with different responses to temperature and photosynthesis in both forest types.

soil respiration fluxes are a combination of CO 2 fluxes derived by different sources and that the relationship of each flux with temperature and photosynthetically derived gross primary productivity is specific to the respirometric source and the vegetation type.
the belowground carbon cycle is tightly linked to aboveground processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the respiration of the different components in soil is affected by photosynthesis, and the time lags between the two processes are different for each ecosystem.
the partitioning of soil CO2 efflux into its components can be achieved with relatively low costs and can provide valuable information on ecosystem carbon flux dynamics.
a better understanding of the mechanisms controlling belowground respiration is needed to predict ecosystem carbon balance and its response to environmental changes.
